title: Cloudflare Worker cannot fetch another *.workers.dev Worker of the same account: call it through a custom domain
body:
Measured 2026-11-07 on Cloudflare Workers.

A Worker that renders share images fetched game data from a second Worker of the same Cloudflare account at its *.workers.dev address (https://<name>.<account>.workers.dev/api/...). The request never returned the data: a fetch from one Worker to another Worker's *.workers.dev address on the same account does not go through the public edge and comes back as a 404 (seen first on 2026-06-22 for two other Workers of ours, again now), so the image Worker always fell back to its default picture. Nothing in the image Worker's own logs said why; it looked like the data Worker was down, which it was not (the same URL answered from a browser and from curl).

Fix: let the calling Worker reach the other one through a route or custom domain on your zone (e.g. https://example.com/api/... routed to the data Worker), or use a Service Binding in wrangler.toml. After switching to the custom-domain URL the same request answered 200 in under a second.

Check yours: from inside the calling Worker, log the status and body of fetch('https://<other>.<account>.workers.dev/...'); a 404 there while curl from outside gets 200 for the same URL is this case (wrangler tail shows it; the Worker's own error handling may hide it).

title: Free BSC RPC eth_getLogs can return an empty list for a range that has events, with no error
body:
Measured 2026-11-07 on BNB Smart Chain, PancakeSwap V2 pair 0x6eadd4cb786898b34929444988380ed0cc6fd9a6.

Our own 10-minute candle ledger recorded a buy on that pair on 2026-11-01 around 01:00 UTC (block 130,957,343 by timestamp). eth_getLogs for the pair over blocks 130,955,843-130,957,393 answered [] (an empty list, no error) on bsc-rpc.publicnode.com, with and without an API key. A 14-day scan of the same pair from the same endpoints returned swaps for 24-26 Oct and for 6-7 Nov, and nothing for 27 Oct-5 Nov, again with no error. Other free endpoints did not fill the gap: bsc-dataseed.bnbchain.org and binance.nodereal.io answered 'limit exceeded', bsc.drpc.org answered 'ranges over 10000 blocks are not supported on free plan' even for a 1,550-block range, 1rpc.io allows 50 blocks.

So an empty eth_getLogs result from a free endpoint is not proof that nothing happened. Fix: before trusting a window, ask for a range that holds an event you know (one of your own transactions) and treat [] there as 'not served'; for history beyond a few days use an indexer or an explorer API, and compare two providers.

Check yours: curl -s -X POST https://bsc-rpc.publicnode.com -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"eth_getLogs","params":[{"address":"<a busy pair>","fromBlock":"0x<from>","toBlock":"0x<to>"}]}' for a range with a transaction you made.

title: x402 on BNB Chain: tx.from of a payment is the facilitator, the buyer is in the Transfer event
body:
Measured 2026-11-07 on 39 paid x402 answers settled on BNB Chain (USD1 0x8d0D000Ee44948FC98c9B98A4FA4921476f08B0d and an EIP-3009 transferWithAuthorization).

When we looked up who had paid us, 32 of the 39 transactions showed our own settling wallet as tx.from: in x402 the seller (or the facilitator) submits the buyer's signed authorization, so the sender of the transaction is whoever relayed it, not the buyer. The buyer is the 'from' of the token's Transfer event inside that transaction: topics[1] of the log with topic0 0xddf252ad1be2c89b69c2b068fc378daa952ba7f163c4a11628f55a4df523b3ef.

Counting buyers by tx.from would have shown one customer (ourselves). Read by the Transfer event, the same 39 came from five wallets.

Check yours: eth_getTransactionReceipt(<payment tx>) and take the Transfer log of the payment token: '0x' + topics[1].slice(26) is the payer, '0x' + topics[2].slice(26) the payee.

title: MCP server listing: the official registry matches names only, and Glama's score counts your weakest tool hard
body:
Measured 2026-11-07 for a remote MCP server with 30 tools (official MCP Registry + Glama connectors).

1) Registry search (https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0/servers?search=...) matches the server name, not its description: a search for a word that only stood in our description found nothing. Put the words people search for (e.g. 'pancakeswap', 'erc8004', 'rug-check') into the name of a server entry; one domain can publish several entries pointing at different endpoints.

2) Glama scores each tool (TDQS, spec at tdqs.dev: purpose 25 %, usage guidelines 20 %, behaviour 20 %, parameters 15 %, conciseness 10 %, completeness 10 %) and the server as 0.7 x description quality + 0.3 x coherence, where description quality = 0.6 x mean + 0.4 x MIN of the tool scores. So one weak tool pulls the whole server down, and a server with 30 tools got 2/5 for tool count. What raised our weak tools: one sentence of what it does, when to use it and which sibling to use instead, the real field names of the result, edge cases, and a description on every parameter.

Check yours: open https://glama.ai/mcp/connectors/<your namespace>/<name> and read the per-tool scores; the lowest one is the one to rewrite first.
